questions.question: What does SNS stand for in AWS?

explanation.correct: SNS stands for Simple Notification Service — a fully managed messaging and notification service in AWS.
explanation.why: SNS enables publishers to send messages to subscribers through topics.

questions.question: In SNS, what is a 'Topic'?

options.text: A communication channel through which publishers send messages to subscribers

explanation.correct: A Topic in SNS is a logical channel or access point that acts as the communication hub — publishers send to it, and subscribers receive from it.
explanation.why: Think of it like a YouTube channel: the creator publishes to the channel and all subscribers receive notifications.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a valid SNS subscription protocol?

explanation.correct: SNS supports Email, HTTP/HTTPS, SMS, SQS, Lambda, and mobile push — FTP is not a supported protocol.
explanation.why: FTP is a file transfer protocol and is not part of SNS subscription options.

questions.question: What is the difference between SNS Standard and FIFO topics?

options.text: FIFO supports email subscriptions; Standard does not
Standard supports all protocols and best-effort ordering; FIFO strictly preserves message order but only supports SQS
FIFO is free; Standard is paid
Standard encrypts messages; FIFO does not

explanation.correct: Standard topics support all protocols (email, HTTP, SMS, etc.) with best-effort ordering. FIFO topics strictly preserve message order but only support SQS as a subscriber.
explanation.why: FIFO = First In First Out — messages are delivered in the exact order they are sent, but the subscriber type is restricted to SQS only.

questions.question: What does CloudWatch primarily do in AWS?

options.text: Monitors and collects metrics, logs, and events from AWS resources and applications

explanation.correct: CloudWatch is AWS's monitoring and observability service — it collects metrics, stores logs, and enables you to set alarms on AWS resources and applications.
explanation.why: Think of CloudWatch as the dashboard in your car, always monitoring speed, fuel, temperature, and warning lights.

questions.question: By default, how often does an EC2 instance send metrics to CloudWatch?

explanation.correct: By default, EC2 instances send metric data to CloudWatch every 5 minutes. Enabling Detailed Monitoring reduces this interval to every 1 minute (additional charges apply).
explanation.why: The default 5-minute interval is called basic monitoring. Detailed monitoring provides 1-minute granularity.

questions.question: What are the three states of a CloudWatch Alarm?

explanation.correct: CloudWatch Alarms have three states: OK (metric is within threshold), In Alarm (metric has breached threshold), and Insufficient Data (not enough data to determine state).
explanation.why: A newly created alarm starts in Insufficient Data, transitions to OK once monitoring begins, and moves to In Alarm if the threshold is breached.

questions.question: What is a CloudWatch metric?

options.text: A text log file stored in S3
A measurement of something over time, such as CPU utilization or request count
An IAM policy attached to a resource

explanation.correct: A metric is a time-series data point that represents a measurement — for example, CPU utilization at 75% over the last 5 minutes, or 1000 requests per minute.
explanation.why: Metrics are the raw data that CloudWatch collects from your AWS resources automatically.

questions.question: What is AWS Lambda?

options.text: A serverless compute service that runs code in response to events without requiring server management
A virtual machine service similar to EC2

explanation.correct: AWS Lambda is a serverless, event-driven compute service. You upload your code as a function, and Lambda automatically provisions the compute resources, runs the code when triggered, and shuts down after execution.
explanation.why: Unlike EC2 where you pay for uptime, Lambda charges only for the time your code actually runs.

questions.question: What is the maximum execution timeout for an AWS Lambda function?

explanation.correct: The maximum execution timeout for a Lambda function is 15 minutes (900 seconds). The default timeout is 3 seconds.
explanation.why: Lambda is designed for short-duration tasks. For long-running workloads (>15 min), use EC2, ECS, or Fargate instead.

questions.question: How are you billed for AWS Lambda?

options.text: Per hour the function is deployed
Based on the number of requests and compute time consumed

explanation.correct: Lambda billing is based on two factors: the number of requests (invocations) and the duration of compute time in milliseconds. You pay only when your code runs.
explanation.why: If your function runs for 55 milliseconds, you pay for 55 milliseconds — not for idle time.

questions.question: What is a Lambda Layer?

options.text: A security boundary between Lambda functions
A reusable component containing dependencies, libraries, or custom runtimes that can be shared across Lambda functions
A network layer that routes traffic to Lambda
A CloudWatch log group for Lambda

explanation.correct: Lambda Layers allow you to package third-party libraries, custom runtimes, or other dependencies separately and share them across multiple functions — avoiding redundant bundling.
explanation.why: If your Python script needs Pillow or Pandas, you create a layer with those packages and attach it to your function instead of including them in your deployment zip.

questions.question: What happens when a CloudWatch Alarm transitions to the 'In Alarm' state and is configured with an SNS action?

options.text: SNS sends a notification to all subscribers of the configured topic

explanation.correct: When a CloudWatch Alarm transitions to In Alarm, it triggers the configured actions — which can include sending a notification via SNS to all subscribers, stopping/starting EC2 instances, or invoking Auto Scaling.
explanation.why: This is the core integration pattern: CloudWatch monitors → alarm triggers → SNS notifies + optional EC2 action.

questions.question: A company wants to automatically rename files uploaded to S3 with a timestamp. Which AWS service combination achieves this with the lowest operational overhead?

options.text: S3 + Lambda (triggered by S3 PUT event)

explanation.correct: Lambda can be triggered by an S3 PUT event. When a file is uploaded, Lambda automatically runs, processes the file, and renames it — no servers to manage, and you only pay for the execution time.
explanation.why: EC2 with a cron job would require continuous billing and manual management. Lambda is the serverless, event-driven choice.

questions.question: What is the purpose of CloudWatch Log Groups?

options.text: To store billing data for AWS accounts
To group and store application logs, system events, and Lambda output for monitoring and analysis
To create dashboards showing EC2 performance

explanation.correct: CloudWatch Log Groups are containers that store log streams from various sources — applications, Lambda functions, EC2 instances, and AWS services. They enable searching, filtering, and setting metric filters on log data.
explanation.why: Lambda automatically creates a Log Group for each function and stores all execution output there.

questions.question: An EC2 instance's CPU is consistently above 80%. You need to receive an email notification. What is the correct service combination?

explanation.correct: Create a CloudWatch Alarm on the EC2 CPU Utilization metric with threshold 80%. Configure it to send notification to an SNS topic with an email subscription. When CPU exceeds 80%, alarm triggers and subscribers receive email.
explanation.why: This is the standard monitoring-to-notification pattern in AWS.

questions.question: What does the 'Detailed Monitoring' option for EC2 provide?

options.text: Enables security scanning of EC2 instances
Reduces metric collection interval from 5 minutes to 1 minute (additional charges apply)

explanation.correct: Detailed Monitoring changes the CloudWatch metric reporting interval from the default 5 minutes to 1 minute, providing near-real-time visibility. However, it incurs additional charges.
explanation.why: Basic monitoring = free, 5-min intervals. Detailed monitoring = paid, 1-min intervals.

questions.question: Which of the following are the four Golden Signals you should monitor for any system?

explanation.correct: The four Golden Signals (from Google's SRE book, and applicable to CloudWatch monitoring) are: Latency (how long requests take), Traffic (how much load), Errors (failure rate), and Saturation (how full/consumed the resource is).
explanation.why: Monitoring these four signals gives a complete picture of system health and is the basis for effective alarm setup.

questions.question: An SNS subscriber must confirm a subscription before receiving messages via which protocol?

explanation.correct: Email subscriptions require explicit confirmation. When you subscribe an email address to an SNS topic, AWS sends a confirmation email, and the subscriber must click the link to confirm before receiving any messages.
explanation.why: This prevents unauthorized email subscriptions. SQS and Lambda subscriptions are confirmed automatically.

questions.question: What is the role of boto3 in Lambda Python functions?

options.text: It is a Python web framework for building REST APIs
It is the AWS SDK for Python that allows Lambda to interact with other AWS services programmatically
It is a testing framework for Lambda functions
It is a package for creating Lambda layers

explanation.correct: boto3 is the official AWS SDK for Python. Inside Lambda, it is pre-installed and allows your code to call AWS services — S3, EC2, DynamoDB, SNS, and more — using Python.
explanation.why: Without boto3, your Lambda code cannot interact with other AWS resources. It is the bridge between your code and AWS APIs.

questions.question: A Lambda function is triggered by an S3 event in the same S3 bucket where it writes its output. What risk does AWS warn about?

options.text: Higher billing due to cross-region data transfer
Recursive invocation — the output triggers the function again, potentially creating an infinite loop
Lambda cannot access the same bucket it is triggered from
S3 event notifications are disabled when Lambda is the target

explanation.correct: If your Lambda writes output to the same S3 bucket that triggers it (without using different prefixes/folders), the output write triggers the function again, which writes again, causing infinite recursive invocations and runaway costs.
explanation.why: AWS warns about this during trigger configuration. Use separate input/output folders (e.g., uploads/ and processed/) to prevent recursion.

questions.question: You want to automatically stop EC2 instances every night at 6 PM without manual intervention. Which is the BEST approach?

options.text: Set a CloudWatch Alarm on CPU utilization to stop the instance
Use AWS Config to detect running instances and stop them
Use Amazon EventBridge (CloudWatch Events) to trigger a Lambda function on a schedule (cron)
Use SNS to send a stop signal to EC2

explanation.correct: EventBridge supports cron-based scheduling. You can create a rule that triggers a Lambda function every day at 6 PM, and the Lambda uses boto3 to call ec2.stop_instances(). This is fully automated and serverless.
explanation.why: CloudWatch Alarms are metric-based (reactive), not time-based (scheduled). EventBridge + Lambda is the correct pattern for scheduled automation.

questions.question: What is the difference between a CloudWatch metric and a CloudWatch log?

options.text: Metrics are paid; logs are free
Metrics are numerical time-series data points (e.g., CPU %); logs are text records of events (e.g., application output, errors)
Logs are only for Lambda; metrics are only for EC2
Metrics are stored in S3; logs are stored in DynamoDB

explanation.correct: Metrics are numerical measurements sampled over time (e.g., CPU at 75% at 10:05 AM). Logs are text-based event records (e.g., 'Error 500 at /api/login'). Both are stored in CloudWatch but serve different purposes.
explanation.why: Use metrics for alerting and dashboards; use logs for debugging and root cause analysis.

questions.question: An EBS volume is being created as GP2, but company policy requires GP3. You need to automatically convert it to GP3 without manual intervention. What is the correct architecture?

options.text: Lambda triggered by CloudTrail/EventBridge on EBS create event → boto3 modifies volume type to GP3

explanation.correct: EventBridge captures the EBS volume creation event via CloudTrail. This triggers a Lambda function that uses boto3 to call modify_volume() and change the type from GP2 to GP3 automatically.
explanation.why: This is a real-world Lambda automation use case: enforce infrastructure compliance without human intervention.

questions.question: Lambda automatically creates a log group in CloudWatch for each function. Where can you view the execution output and errors?

options.text: S3 bucket named after the function
SNS topic subscribed to the function

explanation.correct: Lambda automatically streams all print() statements, exceptions, and execution metadata to a CloudWatch Log Group named /aws/lambda/[function-name]. Each invocation creates a log stream inside that group.
explanation.why: This is the primary debugging tool for Lambda. Always check CloudWatch Logs when a Lambda function fails.

questions.question: What is the maximum memory you can allocate to a Lambda function?

explanation.correct: Lambda supports memory allocation from 128 MB to 10,240 MB (10 GB). The amount of memory you allocate also proportionally scales the CPU power available to your function.
explanation.why: More memory = more CPU. If your function is CPU-bound (image processing, ML inference), increase memory to get more CPU, even if you don't need the extra RAM.

questions.question: A CloudWatch dashboard is BEST described as:

options.text: An S3 bucket that stores metric data
A customizable, shareable view of CloudWatch metrics and alarms across multiple resources and regions

explanation.correct: CloudWatch Dashboards let you create custom views combining metrics from multiple services (EC2, RDS, Lambda, etc.) in different formats (line graphs, numbers, gauges) — all in one screen for real-time visibility.
explanation.why: Dashboards are the operational control center for your AWS environment, enabling at-a-glance health monitoring.

questions.question: Which CloudWatch alarm action allows automatic remediation when CPU utilization exceeds 90%?

options.text: Send email only — CloudWatch cannot take automated actions
Trigger SNS notification AND/OR take EC2 actions (stop, terminate, reboot) AND/OR trigger Auto Scaling
Automatically create a new IAM role

explanation.correct: CloudWatch Alarms support multiple action types: SNS notifications, EC2 instance actions (stop, start, reboot, terminate), and Auto Scaling policies — all configurable per alarm, combinable in a single alarm.
explanation.why: This multi-action capability makes CloudWatch Alarms a powerful automation trigger, not just a notification tool.

questions.question: What is the temporary storage limit for a Lambda function's /tmp directory?

explanation.correct: Lambda provides a /tmp directory for temporary file storage. The default size is 512 MB, configurable up to 10,240 MB (10 GB). This storage is ephemeral — it is cleared after the function execution environment is recycled.
explanation.why: Use /tmp for intermediate file processing (e.g., downloading a file, processing it, uploading the result). Do not rely on /tmp for persistent storage between invocations.

questions.question: A Lambda function that processes images needs the Pillow library. The library is too large to include in the deployment package (50MB limit). What is the correct solution?

options.text: Create a Lambda Layer with Pillow installed, attach it to the function
Deploy the function on EC2 instead
Use inline code editor in AWS Console

explanation.correct: Lambda Layers solve the dependency size problem. Install Pillow in a directory, zip it, upload as a Layer, and attach the Layer to your function. The function can then import Pillow normally, and the layer counts against a separate 250 MB limit.
explanation.why: The deployment package limit is 50 MB (zipped) or 250 MB (unzipped). Layers have their own 250 MB unzipped limit and are shared across functions.

questions.question: Which statement about SNS Fan-out pattern is correct?

options.text: One SNS topic can only have one subscriber
One message published to an SNS topic is delivered to all subscribers simultaneously, enabling parallel processing
SNS fan-out requires SQS FIFO queues only
Fan-out is only supported in SNS FIFO topics

explanation.correct: SNS Fan-out allows a single published message to be simultaneously delivered to multiple subscribers (SQS queues, Lambda functions, HTTP endpoints, emails). This enables parallel, independent processing of the same event.
explanation.why: Example: An order placed triggers SNS, which simultaneously notifies the billing system (SQS), shipping system (Lambda), and customer (Email) — all from one publish call.

questions.question: What is the default Lambda timeout, and what is the maximum?

explanation.correct: The default Lambda timeout is 3 seconds. The maximum configurable timeout is 15 minutes (900 seconds). If your function exceeds the configured timeout, AWS terminates it and returns a timeout error.
explanation.why: Always set your timeout based on realistic execution time, not the maximum. Unnecessarily high timeouts waste money if bugs cause infinite loops.

questions.question: An SNS topic has subscribers: SQS queue, Lambda function, and an email address. A message is published. What happens?

options.text: Only the first subscriber receives the message
Messages are delivered to subscribers one at a time in round-robin
All three subscribers receive the same message simultaneously
The message is queued until all subscribers acknowledge it

explanation.correct: SNS uses a push model — when a message is published to a topic, SNS immediately pushes it to ALL subscribers simultaneously, regardless of type (SQS, Lambda, email, HTTP). This is the fan-out pattern.
explanation.why: This parallel delivery is what makes SNS powerful for event-driven architectures requiring multiple consumers.

questions.question: Which AWS service provides billing alarm functionality and in which region must it be configured?

options.text: CloudWatch Billing Alarm — must be created in us-east-1 (N. Virginia)

explanation.correct: CloudWatch Billing Alarms are a special alarm type only available in the us-east-1 (N. Virginia) region, because AWS billing data is aggregated there. You must switch to this region to create or view billing alarms.
explanation.why: This is a common exam trap. Billing alarms are NOT available in other regions like Mumbai or London.

questions.question: What does it mean when Lambda is described as 'auto-scaling'?

options.text: Lambda automatically increases EC2 instance size
Lambda automatically provisions more concurrent execution environments as request volume increases, with no manual configuration
Lambda uses Auto Scaling Groups to manage capacity
Lambda scales memory manually based on CloudWatch metrics

explanation.correct: Lambda scales automatically and concurrently. If 1000 requests arrive simultaneously, Lambda can spin up to 1000 parallel execution environments (subject to account concurrency limits). You never configure scaling — it happens automatically.
explanation.why: This is fundamentally different from EC2 Auto Scaling, which requires configuration, launch templates, and warm-up time. Lambda scaling is instant and automatic.
